questions.q: Why isn't the budget alert itself enough to resolve this cost spike?
options: It confirms that spending crossed a threshold but doesn't identify which specific resource is responsible for the spend
Budget alerts in Azure never actually report accurate spending figures
The alert only fires after the full budget has already been exceeded, so it's too late to act
Budget alerts can only be configured for an entire subscription, never a resource group
questions.explain: The alert tells you that spending is high and roughly by how much, but finding the actual cause requires a cost-by-resource breakdown, which is a separate step.

questions.q: What does grouping the Cost Management query by ResourceId (az costmanagement query --dataset-grouping name=ResourceId) let you see that the budget alert alone doesn't?
options: Actual cost broken down per individual resource, so one disproportionately expensive resource stands out from the rest
The physical datacenter location of each resource
A list of every RBAC role assigned in the resource group
Which NSG rules are currently blocking traffic
questions.explain: Grouping cost by ResourceId ranks spend per resource rather than just totaling the resource group, which is exactly what surfaces loadtest-vm1 as the outlier.

questions.q: What two separate problems does the investigation find with loadtest-vm1?
options: It's an oversized VM (Standard_D4s_v3) left running continuously, and its OS disk is provisioned at the Premium_LRS tier for a non-production workload
It has no public IP and is missing an NSG rule
It belongs to the wrong resource group and has no tags applied
It was never actually created, despite appearing in the cost report
questions.explain: Both the VM size and the disk's performance tier are oversized for what the VM is actually used for — a dev/test load-testing box, not a production workload.

questions.q: What does az vm deallocate accomplish that simply stopping the VM from within its own operating system would not?
options: It stops compute billing for the VM, whereas an OS-level shutdown leaves the VM still allocated and still billing for compute
It permanently deletes the VM and all of its disks
It changes the VM's size automatically to the cheapest available option
It has no effect on billing either way — only deleting the VM stops compute charges
questions.explain: Deallocating releases the compute allocation and stops compute billing; a VM merely shut down from inside the OS can still be allocated and still billing.

questions.q: Why is StandardSSD_LRS a more appropriate disk SKU for loadtest-vm1 than Premium_LRS, according to this lesson?
options: Premium_LRS is priced for low-latency production workloads, and loadtest-vm1 is a dev/test box that doesn't need that performance tier
StandardSSD_LRS is required for any VM smaller than Standard_D4s_v3
Premium_LRS disks cannot be attached to VMs outside of production resource groups
There is no practical difference between the two SKUs other than the name
questions.explain: Premium_LRS costs more because it's built for latency-sensitive production use; a dev/test load-testing VM doesn't need that tier and StandardSSD_LRS is the appropriate, cheaper match.
